newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh silk factory eyes overseas markets.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh silk factory eyes overseas markets.

text.p: Bangladesh's Rajshahi Silk Factory is facing tough challenges from growing trade unionism, worn out machinery, local buyers' lack of money for its products and the threat of new competition.

Like the machinery, many of the factory's more than 400 employees have become old, but they cannot be retired because the factory is unable to pay their pensions unless the government sanctions a special fund.
Trade union leaders are involved with the management in day-to-day administration of the mill and often dictate terms for recruitment and development.
But the factory's Manager, Mohammad Abu Tahir, said he would not give up easily.
"There is no denying that not even five percent of Bangladesh's 120 million people can afford to buy silk," he told Reuters at his factory recently.
"(But) that does not really spell doom for our future. We can look overseas and internationalise our products," he said.
"This will keep us alive."
The Rajshahi Silk Factory is one of two factories run by the state's Bangladesh Sericulture Board (BSB).
As Tahir spoke, M. Abu Salim, president of the central bargaining agents of the BSB, sat beside and often interjected to explain his ideas.
"They (trade unions) can't be ignored. They have to be handled in a decent, careful, persuasive way," Tahir said.
The factory currently produces only about 100,000 metres of silk cloth annually -- far lower than demands from Japan, Malaysia and other countries.
Tahir said his factory would raise its production to 460,000 metres by 1999, of which 400,000 metres would be for export.
"We are not making any significant strides in the export business despite the overseas demand," he said.
The rest would meet domestic requirements, including silk sarees worn by female cabin crew of the Bangladesh airline Biman.
A second BSB-run silk factory is located at Thakurgaon, also in the north, which has set a 100,000-metre production target for 1998.
Tahir and BSB officials are worried because the government had already decided to allow formation of a non-government Silk Foundation financed by the World Bank.
"This will be a private parallel of the BSB and may drain its experts as the foundation would probably offer much higher salaries and benefits," one BSB official said without elaborating.

"The government says the foundation will improve production and marketing of Bangladeshi silk abroad. Can't they (the government) divert the World Bank funds to us to ensure better management, expansion and higher production?" said the BSB official.
Tahir, despite his reservations, said he welcomed competition.
"I like competition for a healthy growth of the industry -- but not from cheaper, low quality Indian silk flooding our markets," he said.

Other factory officials said the minimum price of a pure silk saree, a five-metre length of cloth worn by women, should be no less that 3,000 taka ($68) but "you can get a silk saree at 700 taka ($16) in our market."

Production of one kilogram of raw silk costs 1,400 taka but the farmers receive 1,200 taka only, officials say. "Such losses are driving many farmers to use their land for producing crops other than mulberry plants for cocoons," said Dr. Abdul Aziz Sarker, a senior research officer at the BSB.

The export volume currently is insignificant, Tahir said. "But we can make the state-run silk industry a multi-million dollar venture through firm government actions and by modernising production units."
Tahir said dozens of smaller private silk factories were being founded with foreign help.
"Unless we can compete strongly our days may be numbered. But I don't think so. We too have a bright future."
